title: Common-Gate Stage
intro: In the common-gate (CG) stage the input drives the source, the output is taken at the drain and the gate is held at a DC bias. It has low input resistance, a non-inverting gain, and is the top half of every cascode (Razavi, Section 3.5).

blocks.alt: Common-gate stage: NMOS M1 with gate at a bias voltage Vb, drain connected to VDD through RD with the output Vout at the drain, and source connected to a current source I1 to ground. The input Vin is coupled to the source through capacitor C1.
blocks.caption: A CG stage biased by a current source, with the input capacitively coupled. The input can also drive the source directly, in which case the bias current flows through the signal source.

blocks.text: With the input driving the source directly, sweep $V_{in}$ down from a high value. For $V_{in} \ge V_b - V_{TH}$, M1 is off and $V_{out} = V_{DD}$. Below that, in saturation,

blocks.tex: V_{out} = V_{DD} - \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_b - V_{in} - V_{TH})^2 R_D

blocks.text: until $V_{out}$ falls to $V_b - V_{TH}$ and M1 enters triode. Since $\partial V_{TH}/\partial V_{in} = \eta$, the small-signal gain is

It is positive, and body effect helps: raising the source raises the threshold, which reduces the current further. For a given current and supply, the gain can be raised by widening M1 (toward subthreshold, where $g_m \to I_D/(\xi V_T)$) or by enlarging $R_D$ and its DC drop; with a current-source bias, $V_{out}$ cannot go below $V_{GS} - V_{TH} + V_{I1}$, where $V_{I1}$ is the minimum voltage the bias source needs. By choice of $V_b$ and $R_D$ the device can be kept saturated for the whole input range ($V_{DD} - R_D I_D > V_b - V_{TH}$ at the largest current), or, impractically, kept in triode throughout ($V_b > V_{DD} + V_{TH}$).

With $\lambda = 0$ the source sees $1/(g_m + g_{mb})$, the same as a follower's output. That low value is the point of the stage: it can terminate a transmission line or accept a current signal. Including $r_o$ changes the picture:

The drain resistance appears at the source divided by the intrinsic gain, which is not much in short-channel devices. With $R_D = 0$ this reduces to the follower result $\frac{1}{g_m + g_{mb}} \parallel r_o$. With an ideal current-source load, $R_{in} \to \infty$: the device current cannot change, so moving the source draws no current. The input resistance is low only if the drain load is low.

A CS device M1 sends its signal current down a $50\,\Omega$ line. Ending the line in a $50\,\Omega$ resistor gives $A_v = -g_{m1} \cdot 50\,\Omega$. Ending it instead at the source of a CG device M2 sized so $1/(g_{m2} + g_{mb2}) = 50\,\Omega$ still terminates the line without reflections, but the signal current now flows on to a drain resistor $R_D$ that can be much larger than $50\,\Omega$: same $-g_{m1}R_D$ form, much higher gain. Keeping M2's capacitance small calls for a small device at a large current, which costs power and $V_{GS}$.
With a source resistance $R_S$ driving the input and $r_o$ included:

This resembles the degenerated CS gain, slightly larger because of body effect. With a current-source load ($R_D \to \infty$) it becomes $A_v = (g_m + g_{mb})r_o + 1$, independent of $R_S$: the source then sees an infinite resistance, so the source node simply follows $v_{in}$. Results can be reused by inspection; for instance, a follower M1 driving the source of a CG device M2 is replaced by its Thevenin equivalent ($v_{in}$ times the follower gain, behind $r_{o1} \parallel \frac{1}{g_{m1}} \parallel \frac{1}{g_{mb1}}$) and plugged into the formula above.
Looking back into the drain, the circuit is a device degenerated by $R_S$:

When the input is a current source $I_{in}$ with its own output resistance $R_P$, replace it by a Thevenin source $I_{in}R_P$ behind $R_P$ and use the same two formulas. This is the CG stage as a current buffer: it takes current at a low impedance and delivers it at a high one.

blocks.title: Input resistance and gain
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0$, $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$, and the source is driven by a signal source with $R_S = 500\,\Omega$ ($\lambda = 0$). Find the overall gain and the input resistance.
solution: $R_{in} = 1/g_m = 500\,\Omega$, which forms a divider of 0.5 with $R_S$.
The stage gain is $g_m R_D = 10$, so overall $5$. The formula $g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S) = 10/2 = 5$ agrees.

blocks.title: Input resistance with a real drain load
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0$, $r_o = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_D = 20\text{ k}\Omega$. Find $R_{in}$. What would it be with an ideal current-source load?
solution: With an ideal current-source load it is infinite.
blocks.answer: About $1.43\text{ k}\Omega$; infinite with an ideal current source.

blocks.title: Sizing a 50-ohm termination
blocks.text: A CG device with $\eta = 0.2$ must present $50\,\Omega$ at its source. What $g_m$ is needed, and what current if it runs at 0.2 V overdrive?

blocks.title: Gain and output resistance
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0.4\text{ mS}$, $r_o = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_S = 500\,\Omega$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the gain and $R_{out}$. Then find the gain with an ideal current-source load.
solution: $(g_m + g_{mb})r_o = 48$. Gain $= \frac{49 \cdot 10\text{ k}\Omega}{20 + 24 + 0.5 + 10\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{490}{54.5} \approx 9.0$ (the simple $g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S)$ gives 10).
blocks.answer: Gain $\approx 9.0$, $R_{out} \approx 8.2\text{ k}\Omega$; 49 with a current-source load.
